title: State v. Scott
description: Whether the district court erred by denying Scott's motion to suppress evidence obtained through his arrest and detention by Belizean police under the "joint venture" exception to the Fourth Amendment's exclusionary rule, and whether there was insufficient evidence to sustain his convictions for first degree murder, use of a deadly weapon, and tampering with physical evidence.
plaintiff_argument: The State of Nebraska (appellee) argued that the district court correctly denied the motion to suppress because U.S. law enforcement's involvement did not constitute a "joint venture" with Belizean police, and that there was sufficient evidence to support all convictions.
defendant_argument: Aldrick Scott (appellant) argued that the evidence from his cell phone should have been suppressed because his arrest and search by Belizean police constituted a "joint venture" with U.S. law enforcement, making the evidence subject to the Fourth Amendment's exclusionary rule, and that there was insufficient evidence to prove premeditated malice for first-degree murder, or the elements for the other charges.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the district court's judgment, rejecting Scott's arguments regarding the motion to suppress and the sufficiency of evidence for his convictions.

title: State ex rel. Hilgers v. Evnen
description: Whether the retroactive application of L.B. 50's new parole eligibility provisions is constitutional, with the Attorney General arguing it constitutes an impermissible commutation and the Secretary of State arguing it does not.
plaintiff_argument: The Attorney General argued that the retroactive application of L.B. 50's new parole eligibility provisions is unconstitutional because it invades the Board of Pardons' commutation power and impermissibly modifies final criminal sentences, effectively acting as a commutation.
defendant_argument: The Secretary of State argued that L.B. 50's new parole eligibility provisions do not result in a commutation and are, therefore, constitutional.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the district court's judgment, finding that the retroactive application of L.B. 50's new parole eligibility provisions does not result in an unconstitutional sentence commutation.

title: N'Da v. Hybl
description: Whether the 'public convenience and necessity' requirement for nonemergency medical transportation services, as outlined in Neb. Rev. Stat. § 75-311(1)(b) and (3), is facially unconstitutional under the Nebraska Constitution's due process, special legislation, and special privileges and immunities clauses.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs, N'Da and Dignity NEMT, argued that the 'public convenience and necessity' requirement was unconstitutional as it created an unlawful trade barrier, protected existing carriers from competition, and did not serve a legitimate state interest, thereby violating their due process, special legislation, and special privileges and immunities rights under the Nebraska Constitution.
defendant_argument: The State argued that the 'public convenience and necessity' requirement was constitutional, served a legitimate state interest in preventing 'destructive competition' and ensuring reliable transportation services, and was rationally related to public health, safety, and welfare.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the district court's rejection of the facial constitutional challenges to the public convenience and necessity requirement, finding it constitutional, but vacated the district court's rulings on the as-applied challenges, determining that declaratory relief was not appropriate for such challenges.

title: State ex rel. Collar v. Evnen
description: Whether a referendum petition seeking to repeal Section 1 of L.B. 1402, which establishes a private education scholarship program, should be withheld from the general election ballot because it allegedly makes an appropriation for state government expense, thus falling under a constitutional exception to the referendum power.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that the referendum petition is legally insufficient and unconstitutional because Section 1 of L.B. 1402 makes an appropriation for the expense of state government, which is exempt from referendum under Article III, Section 3 of the Nebraska Constitution, and therefore the Secretary of State has a clear duty to withhold it.
defendant_argument: The defendant, the Secretary of State, initially determined the referendum met legal sufficiency requirements but later changed his mind, agreeing with the plaintiff that the referendum is invalid because L.B. 1402 makes appropriations for the expense of state government. The intervenors argued that Section 1 of L.B. 1402 makes no appropriation, or if it does, it is not for the expense of state government, and therefore the referendum is a proper subject for a vote.
decision_outcome: The court denied the writ of mandamus and dismissed the petition, concluding that Section 1 of L.B. 1402 does not make an appropriation and therefore the constitutional exception to the referendum power does not apply.

title: State ex rel. Elizabeth Constance v. Evnen
description: Whether a ballot initiative titled "Protect Women and Children," proposing to protect unborn children from abortion in the second and third trimesters with exceptions, violates the single subject rule or creates voter confusion, and thus should be withheld from the general election ballot.
plaintiff_argument: The relators argued that the second initiative violated the single subject rule and created voter confusion, and that if the first initiative was withheld, the second should also be withheld based on consistent constitutional application.
defendant_argument: The respondent asserted that the intervenors could defend the initiative's inclusion on the ballot. The intervenors argued that the relators' claims were unripe and did not present an actual case or controversy, and that the initiative did not violate the single subject rule.
decision_outcome: The court denied the relators' application for a writ of mandamus, concluding that the second initiative does not violate the single subject rule and will appear on the November 2024 general election ballot.

title: State ex rel. Brooks v. Evnen
description: Whether a ballot initiative proposing to amend the Nebraska Constitution to include a fundamental right to abortion violates the single subject rule or contains confusing language, thereby warranting its removal from the ballot.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued the ballot initiative violates the single subject rule by combining dissimilar propositions and contains misleading, vague, and confusing language that would confuse voters, seeking a writ of mandamus to remove it from the ballot.
defendant_argument: The intervenors (sponsors of the Initiative) argued the initiative is not complex, contains only one subject, and its provisions are naturally and necessarily related to the general subject of creating a constitutional right to abortion. The Secretary of State did not take a position but showed cause why the writs should not issue.
decision_outcome: The court denied the writs of mandamus requested by the relators, ruling that the ballot initiative does not violate the single subject rule and can proceed to the ballot.

title: Joshua M. v. State
description: Whether the State of Nebraska, through the Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS), is immune from negligence claims arising from physical and sexual abuse in foster care under the State Tort Claims Act's (STCA) exemption for claims arising out of assault or battery, with the plaintiff arguing against immunity based on negligent supervision and non-assault abuse, and the defendant arguing for immunity based on the STCA exemption.
plaintiff_argument: The siblings argued that their negligence claims against DHHS for failing to protect them from physical and sexual abuse in foster care fell outside the STCA's assault/battery exemption, relying on prior precedent (Koepf) and asserting that their claims included distinct non-assault abuse.
defendant_argument: DHHS argued that the siblings' claims fell squarely within the STCA's exemption for "any claim arising out of assault [or] battery" and were therefore barred by sovereign immunity, relying on the Moser precedent.
decision_outcome: The court vacated the judgment of the district court as to DHHS and remanded the cause with directions to dismiss the claims against DHHS, while affirming the monetary judgment against the foster parent, Miles.

title: State v. Gnewuch
description: Whether Neb. Rev. Stat. § 29-2292, which allows for deferred judgments, is constitutional under the Nebraska Constitution's separation of powers clause.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, Gnewuch, argued that the deferred judgment statute is constitutional and the district court erred in refusing to consider his motion for a deferred sentence.
defendant_argument: The defendant, the State, argued that the deferred judgment statute is unconstitutional because it violates the separation of powers by allowing the judiciary to invade the executive's prosecutorial discretion.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the district court's judgment, vacated Gnewuch's sentence, and remanded the cause for the district court to consider Gnewuch's motion for deferred judgment, finding the deferred judgment statute constitutional.

title: Planned Parenthood of the Heartland, Inc. v. Hilgers
description: Whether L.B. 574, which regulates both abortion and gender-altering care, violates the single subject requirement of Neb. Const. art. III, § 14.
plaintiff_argument: Planned Parenthood argued that L.B. 574 fails the single subject test because it is impossible to identify a single main purpose without it being too broad, and it improperly combined two distinct legislative subjects (abortion and gender-altering care) to ensure passage.
defendant_argument: Hilgers argued that L.B. 574's subject is "public health and welfare" as stated in its title, and all provisions, including those regulating abortion and gender-altering care, are germane to this broad subject. He also argued that the single subject challenge was nonjusticiable.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the district court's decision, ruling that L.B. 574 does not violate the single subject requirement of Neb. Const. art. III, § 14.

title: Lancaster County Board of Equalization v. Moser
description: Whether the Tax Equalization and Review Commission (TERC) erred in ordering the Lancaster County Board of Equalization to revalue the Mosers' irrigated cropland as dryland cropland for tax years 2018 and 2019, with the County Board arguing TERC's decision was incorrect and the Mosers arguing it was necessary for tax equalization.
plaintiff_argument: The Lancaster County Board of Equalization (appellant) argued that TERC erred in reducing the valuation of Mary's Farm because there was no clear and convincing evidence of systematic intentional will or failure of plain legal duty, and that replicating an isolated error would have far-reaching negative consequences.
defendant_argument: The Mosers (appellees) argued that their irrigated acres were valued higher than comparable, misclassified irrigated acres on a nearby property, and that the County Board had a plain legal duty to equalize assessments to ensure uniform and proportionate taxation.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed TERC's decision, finding that TERC erred in ordering the revaluation of Mary's Farm's irrigated cropland as dryland cropland for the 2018 and 2019 tax years, and remanded the matter with directions to affirm the County Board's original assessments.
